message.content:
Below is a concise summary of the key rights and protections you have as a residential tenant in Texas. (This is not legal advice; if you need help with a specific situation, consult an attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.) | Area | What the law says | Practical tips | |------|-------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | Landlords may charge up to one month’s rent for a furnished unit and two months’ rent for an unfurnished unit. | Keep a written receipt when you pay the deposit. Ask for a written itemized list of any deductions at move‑out. | | **Move‑in Inspection** | You should receive a written “move‑in condition report” (or a copy of the lease’s condition clause). | Take photos or video of existing damage before you sign the lease. Sign the inspection sheet or note that you agree with it. | | **Habitability** | Landlords must keep the premises safe, sanitary, and in good repair (e.g., plumbing, heating, electrical, pest control). | Report problems promptly in writing. If the landlord fails to fix serious issues, you may withhold rent or pursue a repair‑and‑deduct claim. | | **Rent Payment** | Rent is due on the date specified in the lease. Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are reasonable. | Pay by check, money order, or electronic transfer and keep proof of payment. | | **Notice Requirements** | • For non‑renewal or termination of a month‑to‑month lease: 30 days’ written notice.
• For a fixed‑term lease: the lease ends automatically unless you give notice per its terms. | Put all notices in writing and keep copies. Send via certified mail or email with read receipt if possible. | | **Eviction Process** | A landlord must serve a written notice (usually 3–30 days depending on the reason) before filing an unlawful detainer action. Evictions cannot be carried out by force or lock‑outs. | If you receive an eviction notice, respond in writing. Attend the court hearing; you can present evidence of habitability or other defenses. | | **Privacy & Entry** | Landlords must give reasonable notice (typically 24 hours) before entering, except in emergencies. | Keep a log of any entries. If the landlord enters without notice, you may file a complaint. | | **Discrimination** | Under federal Fair Housing laws and Texas statutes, landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income. | Keep records of any discriminatory remarks or actions. File a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. | | **Lease Modification** | Either party can modify the lease in writing. Oral modifications are generally enforceable but harder to prove. | Get any changes signed by both parties. Keep copies. | | **Right to Repair & Deduct** | If the landlord fails to fix major repairs within a reasonable time, you may repair the issue yourself and deduct the cost from your rent (up to the amount of the rent). | Document the problem, send a written request, keep receipts, and notify the landlord of the deduction. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | You have the right to live without unreasonable interference from the landlord or other tenants. | Report disturbances or harassment in writing. | | **Legal Remedies** | You can sue for unpaid rent, damages, or breach of lease. Small claims court handles disputes under $10,000. | Gather all documentation (lease, receipts, correspondence). Consider mediation first. | ### Where to Get Help | Resource | How it helps | |----------|--------------| | **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection Division** | Provides consumer guides and can investigate landlord complaints. | | **Texas Commission on Human Rights** | Handles discrimination complaints. | | **Local Tenant‑Rights Organizations** | Offer free or low‑cost legal clinics, workshops, and referrals. | | **Small Claims Court** | Quick, inexpensive venue for disputes under $10,000. | | **Legal Aid Societies** | Free legal representation for qualifying low‑income residents. | --- #### Quick Checklist Before Signing a Lease 1. **Read the entire lease** – look for clauses on deposits, maintenance responsibilities, and notice periods. 2. **Ask for a written move‑in inspection** – take photos/video. 3. **Confirm the security deposit limit** – one or two months’ rent. 4. **Verify the landlord’s contact information** – phone, email, address. 5. **Check for “no‑late‑fee” clauses** – some leases waive late fees. If you have a specific question—like how to handle a landlord who refuses to make repairs, or what to do if you receive an eviction notice—feel free to ask!

But we might also offer to generate a contract. The user didn't ask for a contract. So we just answer. No tool needed.
